analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary cutoff for overtime exemption and updates it automatically each year.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2026 with 28 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, where no markup or vote has been held.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, salaried workers labeled executive, administrative, or professional get no overtime pay no matter how little they earn or how many hours they work [S2]. This bill sets a minimum salary a worker must be paid to be denied overtime, starting at $45,000 and rising to $75,000 by 2029, then automatically tracking the 55th percentile of salaried earnings each year without needing a new rulemaking [S2]. It also tightens the limit on nonexempt work from 40% to 20% of an exempt employee's time, so working managers who mostly do frontline work would become overtime-eligible [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning between their current pay and the rising threshold — typically assistant managers, supervisors, and office staff in retail, restaurants, banking, and insurance — who work more than 40 hours a week. Once a worker's salary falls below the threshold, the employer must pay them overtime (1.5x their hourly rate) for hours over 40, or hire enough staff to keep hours down [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a rising salary floor for the overtime exemption: $45,000 on enactment, $55,000 in 2027, $65,000 in 2028, and $75,000 in 2029, so workers below these levels must be paid time-and-a-half after 40 hours [S2].

After 2030 the threshold automatically updates each year to the 55th percentile of national weekly earnings for full-time salaried workers, without requiring a new regulatory process, so it does not erode over time the way past thresholds did [S2].

Cuts the share of nonexempt work an exempt employee may perform from 40% to 20%, meaning salaried 'managers' who spend most of their time doing frontline or clerical work would qualify for overtime [S2].
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly regional data on salaried weekly earnings, making the threshold's basis publicly visible [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently classify large numbers of salaried workers as exempt — retail and restaurant chains, banks, insurance companies, and small businesses with working managers — would owe overtime pay or need to limit hours. Some may convert workers to hourly positions or cut base pay to stay within budget [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail, restaurant, and other salaried-workforce employers

drawbacks.text: A single national threshold rising to the 55th percentile applies the same in low-cost and high-cost regions, so employers in cheaper labor markets could face the largest cost jumps and may reclassify salaried workers to hourly roles with less schedule flexibility [S2].

Narrowing nonexempt duties to 20% of work time reduces the flexibility that lets a salaried manager step onto the floor when staffing is short; employers facing the rule may instead limit managers' hours or add headcount costs they pass to prices or reduced hiring [S2].
Raising the cost of salaried managerial labor gives employers a reason to keep more workers below the threshold, so some workers could see base pay held down or hours capped as firms adjust [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: millions of salaried workers logged as 'exempt' routinely work 50- and 60-hour weeks for straight pay, and a rising threshold returns overtime to the ones who earn the least. The costs are genuine but secondary — overtime liability for employers, some conversion of salaried roles to hourly, and pressure on firms in low-wage regions. The design mitigates the classic weakness of past thresholds (they sat unchanged for years and eroded) by indexing to wages automatically. The strongest good-faith objection is the abrupt ramp: reaching $75,000 within three years could force rapid restructuring in retail and food service rather than a gradual transition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 18, 2026, joined by 28 Democratic cosponsors including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer [S2][S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral remains the last action in the record [S4].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically alive but has not moved [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay salaried workers below the proposed thresholds are better off as things stand, because they continue to pay no overtime for those employees' long hours while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers paying salaried staff no overtime

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record is a Democrat or independent — 28 Democratic cosponsors plus Sanders — and no Republican has signed on, in a Senate where Republicans hold the majority.

industries.note: These employers rely heavily on salaried 'assistant manager' titles to staff long-hours stores and restaurants without overtime; the rising threshold and the 20% nonexempt-work cap would make many of those managers overtime-eligible, raising labor costs or forcing shorter schedules. Their savings come directly out of workers' unpaid overtime.

industries.industry: Banks, insurance, and salaried white-collar employers generally
industries.note: Salaried administrative and professional staff earning under the threshold would become entitled to time-and-a-half after 40 hours, adding payroll costs for firms that currently schedule them over 40 at straight salary.

Owner-operated businesses would face the same overtime rules for under-threshold salaried managers as large chains, with less ability to absorb the cost, though they could also reclassify workers to hourly pay.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee in May of the second year of a Congress rarely move if the committee chair's party has no cosponsor on them. With no Republican support, no scheduled markup, and less than eight months left in the session, the realistic path is that the bill dies quietly at the end of this Congress unless labor-committee politics change; a similar overtime-threshold regulation issued by the Labor Department in 2024 was struck down by a federal court, so congressional action was the proposed alternative route.
